entries.definition: How many waves fit in one centimetre, in cm⁻¹: the higher it is, the more energy the light has.
The range from 4000 to 400 cm⁻¹, where the fundamental vibrations of molecules fall.
The fraction of light that gets through the sample; as a percentage it is %T.
A measure of how much light the sample holds back: A = −log₁₀T, and it grows with the amount of substance.
A = ε·b·c: absorbance is proportional to the light path and to the concentration.
The periodic motion of atoms around their equilibrium positions.
A vibration in which all atoms oscillate together, at the same frequency and in phase.
The number of modes of a molecule: 3N−6 if it is not linear, 3N−5 if it is linear (N = number of atoms).
The stiffness of the «spring» of a bond: it grows from single to double to triple bonds.
m₁m₂/(m₁+m₂): the «effective» mass that oscillates when two atoms are bonded.
The ideal-spring model: evenly spaced levels and a wavenumber proportional to √(k/μ).
The departure from the ideal spring: levels get closer as they go up and weak overtones become possible.
The condition for a transition to be allowed: in IR the dipole must change during the vibration.
The separation of charge in a molecule; to absorb IR it must oscillate with the vibration.
A mode is IR-active if it absorbs infrared, inactive if not (like the symmetric stretch of CO₂).
Two bonds lengthen and shorten together.
One bond lengthens while the other shortens; it usually falls at higher wavenumbers than the symmetric one.
The angle between bonds changes, not their length.
In-plane bending: the H–X–H angle opens and closes.
In-plane bending: the group swings as a block from side to side.
Out-of-plane bending: the group tilts back and forth all together.
Out-of-plane bending: one atom moves forward while the other moves back.
Aromatic hydrogens move out of the ring plane; the position depends on how the ring is substituted.
The ring expands and contracts uniformly; it is a concept, not a diagnostic band in IR.
The jump from level 0 to level 1 of a mode: the strongest band of that mode.
The jump from 0 to 2, to 3…: it is weak and falls a little below twice, three times… the fundamental.
Two modes excited together: the band falls near the sum of their wavenumbers.
Two levels of the same symmetry and close energy mix, repel each other and share the intensity.
Two oscillators sharing an atom vibrate as a pair, in a symmetric and an asymmetric way.
An X–H···Y interaction that lowers and broadens the X–H band.
An alternation of double bonds that lowers the wavenumber of C=O.
In small rings the C=O is stiffer and falls at higher wavenumbers.
Above about 1500 cm⁻¹: few bands, easier to assign.
Below about 1500 cm⁻¹: many coupled bands, typical of the single molecule (some sources say 1300–650).
A protonated amine (for example a hydrochloride): it gives a broad N–H⁺ band between 3200 and 2300 cm⁻¹.
The unprotonated form of the amine: without the wide N–H⁺ envelope.
The same molecule packed in different ways in the crystal: the solid's spectrum changes.
Splits the beam into two arms, one fixed and one moving, and then recombines them.
A half-reflecting plate that sends half of the light into each arm.
The difference in path between the two arms: twice the displacement of the moving mirror.
The detector signal as a function of the optical path difference.
The peak of the interferogram where the path difference is zero and all waves are in phase.
A red laser that measures where the mirror is and decides when to sample the signal.
The calculation that turns the interferogram into a spectrum.
All frequencies are measured together: less noise in the same time.
With no slits, more light reaches the detector.
The wavenumber scale is tied to the laser, so it is very precise.
The smallest distance between two bands that can still be told apart: about 1/maximum OPD.
A function that tapers the edges of the interferogram and the side lobes, at the cost of slightly wider bands.
Adding zeros to the interferogram: the spectrum is smoother but the resolution does not change.
Corrects the asymmetry of a real interferogram before the transform.
The raw spectrum: source, optics, sample and detector together.
The single-beam spectrum measured without the sample: it is needed for the ratio.
The average of several scans: noise falls with the square root of the number of scans.
The infrared source: a silicon carbide rod heated to about 1200 K.
A pyroelectric detector that works at room temperature: linear and widely used.
A detector cooled with liquid nitrogen: faster and more sensitive.
A measurement by contact with a crystal, without preparing the sample.
The field that reaches a few micrometres beyond the surface of the ATR crystal.
The distance at which the evanescent field falls to 1/e: it grows with wavelength.
